authoredPrompt: This figure sets three side-by-side panels, (a), (b), and (c), showing one small undirected graph and two ways of storing it. Panel (a) draws the graph as five gray circles numbered 1 through 5, with 1 at the upper left, 2 at the upper right, 3 at the far right, 4 at the lower middle, and 5 at the lower left, joined by seven straight edges: 1-2, 1-5, 2-5, 2-3, 2-4, 3-4, and 4-5. Panel (b) gives the adjacency-list form as a vertical array of five gray cells indexed 1 to 5, each holding a pointer arrow into a horizontal chain of two-field records whose right field is either an arrow onward or a diagonal slash marking the end. Row 1 chains 2 then 5; row 2 chains 1, 5, 3, 4; row 3 chains 2 then 4; row 4 chains 2, 5, 3; row 5 chains 4, 1, 2. Panel (c) gives the adjacency matrix as a bordered five-by-five grid of zeros and ones with rows and columns both headed 1 through 5, zeros along the diagonal and entries symmetric across it. Laying the picture beside the two tables lets a single edge be found three ways, and it makes plain that each undirected edge is stored twice.
authoredInteractions:
- Click for edge lookup: click an edge in the graph or a 1 in the matrix, and the two adjacency-list entries plus the symmetric matrix cells highlight, showing how one undirected edge is stored twice.
- Toggle between representations: switch focus among graph, adjacency list, and adjacency matrix, and the selected vertex's neighbors highlight across all panels, clarifying that the three views encode the same relationships.
- Button for adding or removing an edge: choose two vertices and press add/remove, and the graph line, both list records, and both symmetric matrix entries update, making the storage consequences of an undirected edge explicit.
authoredContext: The adjacency-list representation of a graph G D .V; E/ consists of an array Adj of jV j lists, one for each vertex in V . For each u 2 V , the adjacency list AdjŒu contains all the vertices _x0017_ such that there is an edge .u; _x0017_/ 2 E. That is, AdjŒu consists of all the vertices adjacent to u in G. (Alternatively, it may contain pointers to these vertices.) Since the adjacency lists represent the edges of a graph, in pseudocode we treat the array Adj as an attribute of the graph, just as we treat the edge set E. In pseudocode, therefore, we will see notation such as G:AdjŒu. Figure 22.1(b) is an adjacency-list representation of the undirected graph in Figure 22.1(a).

discrepancies: The generated default page devotes a large right-side control panel to UI, so the three textbook panels are rendered much smaller than in the source and no longer read as a clean drop-in static figure.

Many labels, matrix digits, adjacency-list row numbers, and subfigure captions are noticeably smaller in the rendered screenshot than the source, making the list and matrix harder to read at inline size.

The adjacency-list pointer column is simplified: the source shows dash-like pointer marks inside the leading array cells, while the generated version mostly renders them as continuous arrow stems from the cells.
The adjacency-list records and arrows are more tightly compressed and uniform than the source, so panel (b) has less of the original textbook spacing and visual weight.
evaluation.notes: The graph topology, adjacency-list contents, and adjacency matrix values match the source very well, but the large UI panel and small rendered labels weaken its faithfulness as a drop-in textbook replacement.
action_items: Make the static figure fill the available width by docking the controls below, collapsing them by default, or otherwise preventing the UI panel from consuming so much horizontal space.
Increase the effective font size and visual scale of the three panels so vertex labels, list entries, matrix digits, and captions are comfortably readable at inline size.
Refine the adjacency-list pointer-column styling to better match the source, including the short dash marks inside the leading cells and the spacing of arrows between records.
